title: How to Start a Tutoring Business: Your 7-Step Guide
summary: Learn how to start a tutoring business in 7 steps, from picking a niche and setting rates to taxes, insurance, and finding your first clients.
body_markdown:
You’ve got students. Maybe three classmates, a neighbor’s kid, and a few families who pay you by Venmo whenever they remember. It works, until a payment goes missing, a session gets canceled twice in one week, or tax season sneaks up on you.


Tutoring is the part you already know, and you’re good at it. What’s missing is the business side: structure, taxes, pricing, and a way to find more clients. Starting a tutoring business takes less money than most ventures, just a handful of smart decisions. Here’s how to start a tutoring business in seven steps.

## **How to Start a Tutoring Business: The Quick Version**


Work through these seven steps in order:


1. **Pick a niche.** Choose a subject and a student group.
2. **Choose a model.** Online, in person, group, or a center.
3. **Make it official.** Start as a sole proprietor and check for licenses.
4. **Handle your money.** Open a bank account, plan for taxes, and consider insurance.
5. **Set your rates.** Compare other tutors and write down your policies.
6. **Find clients.** Start with people who already trust you.
7. **Grow.** Raise rates, add group sessions, then hire.


Curious about pay? The FAQ has you covered.


## **Step 1. Pick Your Tutoring Niche and Student Group**


Parents hire for a specific need, so a clear niche makes you easier to find and easier to choose. Your first students usually show you what yours is.


If you want to know how to start your own tutoring business, this is the first move. “AP Chemistry for juniors” or “SAT math for first-time test takers” gives a parent a reason to pick you over a general homework helper. Three questions help you choose:


- **What can you teach well?** Stick with subjects where you earned strong grades and can explain the why.
- **Who do you enjoy working with?** Middle schoolers, high schoolers, and adults each need a different approach.
- **What pays?** Test prep tends to earn the most.


Your current students are a great place to look. Which subjects do they ask for, and which families send their friends your way?


### **What Qualifications Do You Need to Tutor?**


Most states don’t require a tutoring-specific license or degree, but parents look for proof you can teach. Strong grades or test scores, references, and a background check build trust fast. Rules vary by location, so check your state and city.


If you’d like a credential, the[National Tutoring Association (NTA)](https://ntatutor.com/certification.html) certifies individual tutors, including private tutors. It asks for membership, training, proof of tutoring hours, and a background check. Your school may offer another route: the[College Reading and Learning Association (CRLA)](https://www.crla.net/) certifies college tutor training programs, so ask your campus tutoring center if it’s CRLA certified.


## **Step 2. Choose Your Tutoring Business Model**


Online and in-person sessions are the cheapest ways to start, and most students add group sessions later. A center or franchise is a much bigger leap, and most people skip it at first.


Your tutoring business model shapes your costs, your schedule, and the students you’ll meet. Here’s how the four compare:


- **Online tutoring.** If you’re wondering how to start an online tutoring business, this is the simplest path. All you need is a video call tool and a quiet space, and your students can live anywhere.
- **In-person tutoring.** You meet at a student’s home, a library, or a coffee shop. It builds trust fast, though travel eats into your day.
- **Group sessions.** You earn more per hour, but it’s harder to tailor each lesson.
- **Tutoring center or franchise.** This path costs the most and comes with the most structure.


Wondering how to start a tutoring business from home, or how to start a tutoring business online? Pick online or in-person sessions, and check your local rules on home-based businesses first.


Rhasaan Sherrill, a[Homebase](https://joinhomebase.com/) client, is a good example of how far a no-building model can go. He owns and directs Beat Box Dance Academy, a dance education business with no studio of its own. “This is a mobile business,” he says, so there’s no “actual building or studio” where classes happen. We’ll check back in on his story in step seven.


### **How Much Does It Cost to Open a Tutoring Center?**


A tutoring center costs far more than tutoring solo. Franchise disclosure documents put total initial investment for brands like Kumon, Mathnasium, and Sylvan Learning at roughly $70,000 to $190,000. Independent centers vary widely by lease and build-out, so get quotes before committing.


Each brand lists its startup costs in a Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD), which the[Federal Trade Commission (FTC)](https://www.ftc.gov/) requires franchisors to provide. A 2024 summary from[1851 Franchise](https://1851franchise.com/8-low-cost-education-franchises-2726095) put Kumon at about $67,000 to $146,000, Mathnasium at about $113,000 to $150,000, and Sylvan Learning at about $86,000 to $187,000. These numbers change yearly, so read each current FDD.


### **Write a One-Page Tutoring Business Plan**


You don’t need a thick document, just a page you’ll actually use. Our guide to[writing a one-page business plan](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/one-page-business-plan) includes a free template and examples you can adapt. For a tutoring business plan, make sure it covers these:


- **Who you serve and what you teach.** Your niche from step one, plus the grade levels or exams you’ll cover.
- **How you deliver it.** Online, in person, or both, and where.
- **Your rate and hours.** Multiply your hourly rate by your weekly hours to set a monthly income goal.
- **Your costs.** Insurance, a video call tool, supplies, and any marketplace fees.
- **Your first-month goal.** Pick a number, like three paying students.


Revisit it after a month and see if there’s anything you’d like to update.


## **Step 3. Make Your Tutoring Business Official**


The legal requirements for a tutoring business are lighter than most people expect. A sole proprietorship, a license check, a name, and an optional tax ID cover the basics.


The[U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA)](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/launch-your-business/#business-structure) says you’re automatically a sole proprietor if you do business without registering another structure, so you may already be official.


### **Do You Need an LLC to Start a Tutoring Business?**


No. You can start as a sole proprietor with no registration. A limited liability company (LLC) separates your personal assets from the business and looks more professional, but it adds state filing fees and paperwork. Consider one when you add tutors or take on more risk.


The SBA suggests talking with an accountant or attorney before you decide. If you’re thinking bigger, like how to start a tutoring company with other tutors on board, an LLC is worth a closer look.


### **Do You Need a License to Start a Tutoring Business?**


Most states don’t require a tutoring-specific license. You may still need a general business license from your city or county, and zoning rules can apply to home-based businesses. Check with your city, county, and state before you take payments. The SBA’s[licenses and permits guide](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/launch-your-business/#licenses-permits) is a good place to start.


### **Choose a Name and Get an EIN**


Strong tutoring business names are easy to spell, easy to search, and available as a domain and social handle. If the name isn’t your own, register a “doing business as” (DBA) name with your state, since most states require you to register a “doing business as” name if you use one.


You may also want an Employer Identification Number (EIN), which is free from the[Internal Revenue Service (IRS)](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number) . With no employees, you generally don’t need one, but it keeps your Social Security number off client forms. You’ll need one once you hire an employee. If you plan to hire contractors instead, our guide to[1099 contractors](https://www.joinhomebase.com/glossary/1099-contractor) covers this.


### Make work manageable.


## **Step 4. Set Up Money, Taxes, and Insurance for Your Tutoring Business**


Getting paid is the fun part, and keeping track of it saves you at tax time. Before your first payment lands, open a separate bank account, set money aside for self-employment tax, plan to pay estimated taxes four times a year, and consider liability insurance.


A business bank account and one payment app for every client make the first step easy, because you’ll always know where each dollar came from.


### **Pay Self-Employment Tax and Estimated Taxes**


As a sole proprietor, you pay self-employment tax once you net $400 or more. The[IRS](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/self-employment-tax-social-security-and-medicare-taxes) sets the rate at 15.3%, which covers 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Because no employer withholds it, you report it on Schedule SE and usually pay estimated taxes four times a year using Form 1040-ES. Three habits make it manageable:


1. **Set money aside.** Move part of every payment into savings the day it arrives.
2. **Estimate each quarter.** Use the Form 1040-ES worksheet, or ask a tax pro for a number that fits you.
3. **File on time.** Include your tutoring income on your tax return.


### **Get Insurance for Your Tutoring Business**


Shopping for insurance for a tutoring business? General liability covers injuries or property damage, while professional liability covers claims about your teaching. Both matter most for in-person sessions and for tutoring minors.


According to[Insureon](https://www.insureon.com/professional-services-business-insurance/cost) , tutors and other low-risk professionals pay about $29 a month for general liability, and professional services businesses pay about $43 a month for professional liability. Treat these as a rough range and get a quote.


## **Step 5. Set Your Tutoring Rates**


Your tutoring rate comes down to three things: what the market pays, how you structure your sessions, and what you keep after costs. Settle your policies early, so they back up the price you set.


### **How Much Should I Charge for Tutoring?**


Most new tutors charge by the hour, based on subject, experience, and local competition. Check five tutors in your subject, price near the middle of that range, and raise your rate as you collect reviews and fill your calendar. Don’t underprice to win your first client.


When you’re deciding how much to charge for tutoring, real examples beat guesses. You can price in three ways:


- **Hourly.** Simple, and a good fit when you’re just starting out.
- **Session packs.** Sell four, eight, or twelve sessions at a small discount to keep clients booked.
- **Monthly rates.** Charge a flat fee for weekly sessions, which makes your income easier to predict.


### **Write Your Policies Before Your First Paid Session**


Clear policies protect your time and keep things friendly with parents. Most conflicts come from surprises, so spell out these five things before session one:


- **Cancellations and no-shows.** Set a notice window, such as 24 hours, and say what happens inside it: a late fee, a charged session, or a make-up session.
- **Payment terms.** Decide when you get paid (before each session, monthly, or when a pack is bought) and how. Payment in advance means you never have to chase anyone.
- **Session length and lateness.** Say how long sessions run, and that a late arrival doesn’t extend the session. Add whether you offer make-ups.
- **Communication.** Pick how parents reach you and how fast you reply. A short progress update after a few sessions keeps parents confident in what they’re paying for.
- **Location and safety.** Name where sessions happen, whether that’s online, at home, or in a public space. For students under 18, ask a parent or guardian to agree to the terms.


Put it all on one page or in a short email, and ask parents to reply “agreed.” If a question comes up later, you’ll both have the answer in writing.


### **A Quick Example of What You Keep**


Your rate isn’t your pay, because prep, messages, and invoices take time too. Here’s a simple example with made-up numbers, so swap in your own.


- **Income:** Six hours a week at $40 an hour, over four weeks, is $960.
- **Costs:** Take out about $30 for liability insurance and $10 for tools and supplies, which leaves $920 before taxes.
- **Time:** Add two hours a week for prep and admin, and your six tutoring hours become eight, or 32 hours a month.
- **Real pay:** $920 divided by 32 hours is about $29 an hour, before taxes.


Taxes come out of that number, so set money aside from every payment (see step 4). If travel time or a marketplace fee shrinks your pay further, you’ve found your cue to raise your rate or add group sessions.


## **Step 6. Find Your First Tutoring Clients**


Your first clients will almost always come from people who already know you, so your outreach can start close to home. Reviews and referrals do the rest.


Not sure how to advertise tutoring services? Work through these from easiest to hardest:


1. **Tell people who already trust you.** Classmates, family friends, and former teachers are your warmest leads.
2. **Post on campus.** Try department boards, class group chats, and student organizations, and check your school’s advertising rules first.
3. **Join local parent groups.** Be helpful first and sell second.
4. **Set up a free Google Business Profile.** It helps local families find you.
5. **Try a tutoring marketplace.** Wyzant, Care.com, Superprof, and Varsity Tutors can bring in first clients, though they often take a cut, so check current fees.
6. **Offer a short intro session.** Then ask happy parents for a review or referral.


Start outreach before the semester and before exam season, when parents look for help.


## **Step 7. Grow Your Tutoring Business**


Tutoring businesses grow in stages, and the last stage changes your job from teaching to managing people. That’s when schedules and paperwork start to matter.


Wondering how to grow a tutoring business? Raise your rates first, since a full calendar usually means your price is too low. Next, add group sessions. If you’re still booked solid, it’s time to bring on other tutors—which also means you’ll need to choose between hiring employees ([W-2](https://joinhomebase.com/blog/1099-w2-employees-what-is-the-difference) ) and[independent contractors](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/how-to-hire-an-independent-contractor) (1099).


Scheduling is where growth gets tricky, because your tutors have classes and exams of their own. Rhasaan Sherrill knows the feeling. He says he used to “print out their schedules and email it to them,” and he didn’t believe there was a clock-in system. Now? ## **Frequently Asked Questions About Starting a Tutoring Business**


### **Is 1 Hour of Tutoring a Week Enough?**


It depends on your goal. One hour a week can help with homework or a single test section. To catch up in a subject, research favors more. The[Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL)](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/tutoring) recommends at least three sessions a week for school tutoring, citing evidence that it beats one or two, though that research covers school programs.


### **What Type of Tutor Makes the Most Money?**


Test prep tutors tend to earn the most. In a 2025[Wiingy analysis](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/09/30/3158961/0/en/sat-prep-tutoring-costs-63-more-than-language-learning-wiingy-study-finds.html) of 3,600 tutors, SAT prep averaged $62/hour, ahead of music ($52), math ($46), coding ($39), and language ($38). Rates vary by city, and the figures come from tutoring marketplaces.


### **How Much Does It Cost to Start a Tutoring Business?**


Starting solo can cost a few hundred dollars. You can often launch for under $500 if you already have a laptop and internet. Typical costs include a video call tool, a payment app, and insurance. Costs rise with in-person space.


### **Is a Tutoring Business Profitable?**


Yes, it can be. Startup costs are low, and tutors set their own rates. For context, the[U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)](https://www.bls.gov/OOH/education-training-and-library/tutors.htm) reports a median of about $20.84 an hour for employed tutors. Your profit depends on hours booked, your rate, fees, taxes, and insurance, so track all five from month one.


## **Start Small, Then Build Your Tutoring Business**


Starting a tutoring business comes down to a few moves: pick a niche, set a rate, and make it easy to get paid. Keep the paperwork light, and add systems when your first tutor joins.
